summaries.summary: MOOCs aim to bridge higher education's social gap, but massive online scaling disrupts co-located, synchronous two-way communication between students and instructors.
MOOC forums enable student discussion and instructor intervention, but high student–instructor ratios prevent monitoring all discussions, motivating systems for selective intervention.
The paper proposes first neural models for instructor intervention prediction, modelling thread structure and post sequences and using attention to infer latent intervention-triggering context.
A thread consists of posts, is intervened if an instructor posted at least once, and intervention prediction is binary classification.
A secondary problem infers the appropriate intervention context as a linear contiguous post series from candidate contexts.
Prior forum work models context through discourse, reply structure, conditional random fields, and attention, while this paper infers general dependencies between a reply and previous context.

Unlike graph structured LSTM and document classification models, this work assumes no explicit reply structure and hierarchically encodes post-thread layout while inferring reply structure with attention.
Prior MOOC intervention work proposed the problem, evaluated baselines across MOOCs, used discourse features, and addressed position bias in Coursera forums.
Prior works did not investigate structure and sequence in threaded discussions, while this paper proposes context-inferring models without preset context lengths that generalise BIBREF0 assumptions.
BIBREF7 is chosen for comparison against a state-of-the-art and competing baselines because BIBREF0's system and data are unavailable.

Evaluation uses 12 MOOC iterations on Coursera.org, includes selected subject-matter sub-forums, omits social and instructor-started threads, normalises labels, replaces tokens, and truncates intervened threads.
The key innovation decomposes intervention prediction into discovering proper reply context and predicting intervention status, implicitly assessing thread context importance or urgency.
Context scope inference predicts whether intervention is necessary without the instructor's reply, using only available posts to identify the most plausible motivating subsequence.
Because the actual instructor intervention is unavailable at decision timing, attention uses surrogate text as the query, with model variants assessing surrogate suitability.
All proposed models hierarchically encode threads by passing GloVe word vectors through an LSTM and using its last layer output as the post vector.
Each post vector passes through another LSTM whose last layer encodes the entire thread, while hidden unit outputs represent contexts as thread snapshots.
The two LSTMs constitute the hierarchical LSTM (hLSTM) model, which serves as the basis for subsequent model exploration.
Instructors attend to specific posts or post series triggering replies, but rarely indicate them, so the secondary objective infers appropriate context from binary thread-level intervention signals.
Contexts are limited to linear contiguous post series starting with the original post, unlike tree or graph-like forums such as Reddit.
Three neural attention variants are proposed based on how instructors might attend and reply: ultimate, penultimate and any post attention models.
Ultimate Post Attention (UPA) uses the post prior to the instructor's reply as a query over contexts, treating the final post as equivalent to the prospective intervention.
If one post is the instructor's reply, the preceding post queries over the contexts, with the model schematic shown in Figure FIGREF12.
The attended context representations are computed as DISPLAYFORM0.
The attended representation is passed through a fully connected softmax layer to yield the binary prediction.
Penultimate Post Attention (PPA) models the ultimate post as having prior posts as potential context, using the penultimate post to maximise available information.
Any Post Attention (APA) relaxes UPA and PPA by letting each post query its previous context and normalising attention weights over different queries.
In APA, the attention context is computed via DISPLAYFORM0.
Baseline and models are evaluated on 12 MOOC discussion forums using 80% training data and held-out 20% test data, reporting positive-class scores and prioritising recall.
Neural models use Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001, cross-entropy loss, per-instance updates, one epoch, 300-dimensional GloVe vectors, and hidden dimension size 128.
Baselines include hierarchical LSTM (hLSTM), a feature-rich BIBREF7 logistic regression classifier, and aggregated hLSTM results using only the last post as context.
On the 12 MOOC dataset, UPA and PPA outperform the neural baseline, with mixed course-level results linked to course size and intervention ratio.
UPA's best performance indicates the instructor's reply context strongly correlates with the previous post's context, consistent with normal conversation structure.
The discussion further investigates models' ability to infer context and its effect on intervention prediction through research questions.
RQ1 asks whether context inference helps intervention prediction.
Ablating attention shows UPA and PPA improve over vanilla hLSTM by 5% and 2% on average, indicating context inference improves prediction over full context.
RQ2 bins threads by length across ml-5, rprog-3 and calc-1, finding UPA better on shorter threads and PPA and APA better on longer threads.
RQ3 asks whether models trained with different context lengths perform better than models trained on a single context length.
Context length regularises test performance; single-length training drops sharply, while a multi-objective loss with context length 3 achieves INLINEFORM1 of 0.45, precision 0.47 and recall 0.43.

The paper predicts instructor intervention by inferring optimal context size, shows structured thread representation beats bag-of-words features, and proposes attention models including APA for varying pedagogical styles.
Recall for longer threads of length greater 2 can still improve, and future work plans an ensemble model or multi-objective loss function.
